content: A systematic review was conducted to evaluate the methods and results of studies on food fortification with vitamin A. The search strategy, executed on April 21, 2016, identified 10,683 records after duplicates were removed. The comparisons included staple foods fortified with vitamin A versus no intervention, fortified foods versus the same unfortified foods, and fortified foods with vitamin A plus other micronutrients versus no intervention or unfortified foods. The outcomes of interest were changes in retinol levels, subclinical and clinical evidence of vitamin A deficiency, morbidity, and mortality. A total of 22 studies were included, conducted in lowand middle-income countries such as Bangladesh, India, the Philippines, South Africa, Zambia, Brazil, China, Mexico, and Thailand. The duration of interventions ranged from 3 to 36 months, and participants included individuals with vitamin A deficiency, those at risk of micronutrient deficiencies, and apparently healthy individuals. Only two studies specifically examined maize flour or meal fortified with vitamin A and other micronutrients compared to unfortified maize flour. In one study conducted in South Africa, 44 malnourished children aged 1–3 years were recruited. Group 1 consumed fortified maize flour containing 56 mg pyridoxine per 150 g of raw maize flour, while Group 2 consumed unfortified maize meal. All children regularly consumed maize porridge two to four times daily, either as soft porridge with milk or stiff porridge with relish. Occasional breastfeeding was reported among children aged 12–18 months. The study found no significant increases in hemoglobin or serum retinol levels. The second trial, conducted in Zambia, provided fortified and unfortified maize flour to 212 adolescents (10–19 years), 157 children (6–59 months), and 118 women (20–49 years) in the Nangweshi refugee camp. Each household received a 400 g ration of 97%-extraction fortified maize meal per registered refugee, regardless of age, during the intervention period from November 2003 to June 2004. The fortified maize meal contained 5 mg folic acid, 35 mg elemental iron, and 20 mg zinc per kg. The fortified meal was blended, bagged, and stored for up to four weeks before distribution. The intervention resulted in a significant reduction in vitamin A deficiency prevalence but no significant change in anemia prevalence among adolescents. Evidence from other fortified food vehicles demonstrated that fortification with vitamin A and other micronutrients reduces subclinical vitamin A deficiency in populations. A Cochrane systematic review was commissioned to assess the efficacy of zinc fortification in staple foods, including maize flour or cornmeal. The search strategy, conducted on April 8, 2015, identified 6,582 references after duplicates were removed. Eight studies involving 709 participants were included, but none used maize flour or cornmeal as the fortification vehicle. The cereals studied included wheat bread, biscuits, breakfast cereals, and rice. Zinc doses ranged from 3 to 40 mg per 100 g of food. Zinc fortification improved serum zinc status when zinc was the sole micronutrient used but showed no significant improvement when combined with other micronutrients. The effects of zinc fortification on growth, cognition, work capacity, or hematological indicators were unclear due to a lack of studies reporting these outcomes. A systematic review assessed the impact of food fortification with vitamin D and/or calcium on health outcomes in the general population. The search strategy, conducted on May 20, 2016, identified 1,203 records, with 876 abstracts screened and 62 full-text articles assessed for eligibility. Thirty-seven trials involving 5,563 participants were included in the meta-analysis. The studies were divided into three analyses: calcium-only fortification, vitamin D-only fortification, and combined fortification with vitamin D and calcium. Primary outcomes included morbidity and mortality, while secondary outcomes included serum or plasma concentrations of vitamin D, calcium, and parathyroid hormone (PTH), bone mineral density, markers of bone resorption, and adverse effects. The most common fortification vehicles were dairy products and fruit juice. No studies included maize flour or cornmeal as the fortification vehicle. Vitamin D fortification, alone or in combination with calcium, significantly impacted serum vitamin D levels, serum PTH levels, and total body bone mineral density in selected population groups, although the evidence quality was low. A review of 201 studies showed that fortification of foods with vitamin A, iron, and multiple micronutrients improved serum micronutrient concentrations and increased hemoglobin levels. Iron fortification significantly increased serum ferritin and hemoglobin concentrations. Folate fortification significantly reduced the incidence of congenital anomalies, such as neural tube defects, without increasing twinning rates. However, the number of studies pooled for zinc and multiple micronutrients in women was low, and findings should be interpreted cautiously. Two studies, conducted in Mexico and South Africa, reported the effects of folic acid fortification of maize flour or cornmeal. Consumption of fortified or unfortified maize flour significantly increased plasma folic acid concentrations compared to baseline. No studies reported on the effects of zinc fortification of maize flour or cornmeal. The quality of direct evidence for critical outcomes ranged from low to very low, as assessed using the GRADE methodology. There was no direct evidence for critical outcomes such as iron deficiency anemia, neural tube defects, zinc status, growth, or adverse effects in children. The guideline development group considered additional factors, including population preferences, trade-offs between benefits and harms, costs, and feasibility, to define the direction and strength of recommendations. Although evidence for maize flour or cornmeal fortification is limited, fortification of other staple foods with zinc, vitamin A, folic acid, vitamin D, and calcium has been associated with significant reductions in deficiency-related outcomes and improvements in population health. Countries can integrate maize flour and cornmeal fortification into national programs to prevent and control micronutrient deficiencies. The choice and concentration of nutrients for fortification should consider the nutritional needs and intake gaps of target populations, usual consumption levels, sensory and physical effects of fortificants, and other ongoing nutrition interventions.
